inline.s: As for the Wheel-Turning Sage King: he transforms the world by the ten good deeds, without waiting for weapons of war, and his majesty subdues the four quarters. He is the foremost man of blessed merit in the human world, and the seven treasures appear to him of themselves, at his pleasure and at ease. The first of them is the wheel treasure; the king rides this wheel and patrols the four quarters, and so is called the Wheel-Turning Sage King. The wheel is of four kinds — gold, silver, copper, and iron. One who obtains the golden wheel is called the Golden Wheel King, and he rules the four great continents. The Silver Wheel King rules the three continents of east, west, and south. The Copper Wheel King rules the two continents of east and south. The Iron Wheel King rules one continent, namely Jambudvīpa in the south. By the power of blessed merit he is endowed with the thirty-two marks, but they lack purity and distinctness, because they are produced by defiled karma of merit, and are not the same as those that appear in the Buddha from the undefiled Dharmakāya.
(Chou) Second, speaking the verse and drawing the conclusion.

Then the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

“Who seeks me by a form,
or seeks me by a sound,
has walked a crooked way —
the Tathāgata he has not found.”

“At that time” marks the moment when the refutation and the explanation had just been completed. These two words are set down so that students should grasp this together with the preceding section; for what the verse says is precisely the reason for what was refuted and what was explained. The word “form” refers collectively to all marks of form, and the thirty-two marks are included within it. The two occurrences of “me” refer to the Tathāgata, that is, to the nature. “Sound” includes the sound of Dharma-teaching. The point is precisely that one must not grasp the various earlier teachings of one suchness and equality and seek them amid words and sounds. What sees form is the eye-consciousness; what hears sound is the ear-consciousness — two consciousnesses are named to cover the rest. In sum, seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing: though their essence is the nature, living beings since beginningless time have turned them into consciousnesses. If now one sees by form and seeks by sound, it is plainly the karma-consciousness at work, clinging to the objects of the six dusts. Yet one hopes by these means to see the Dharmakāya, by these means to seek the Dharmakāya — obviously a deluded view, obviously a chasing outward. One’s knowledge and views are already greatly incorrect; how much more so if one still hopes to see the Dharmakāya Tathāgata? Hence the rebuke: “such a one walks a crooked path and cannot see the Tathāgata.” For the nature of true suchness is not the realm of the discriminating, clinging karma-consciousness. The conclusion is drawn to show that one who would contemplate one suchness must first empty out all feeling and consciousness.

Someone may ask: the Buddhist scriptures often tell people to contemplate the Buddha’s marks and excellences — why is that? You should know that this is skillful means. The term “skillful means” carries two senses. Since living beings cling to marks everywhere, they are told to abandon the defiled and contemplate the pure — this is the first sense. Once they know how to contemplate the pure, they are further led onward to the ultimate, as stated here — this is the second sense. To lead one on step by step into the wonder is what is meant by skillful means. That is why in the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations the most essential passage is the several lines: “This mind is the Buddha; this mind makes the Buddha.” When one understands that all is mind-only, one knows that even while contemplating marks and excellences one does not take them as real, and the feeling-consciousness of discrimination and clinging is dismissed. This is also why a reciter of the Buddha’s name, though he may contemplate Amitābha appearing before him and the Pure Land appearing before him, must not cling to them. Why? Because marks are made by the mind. The pure mind of self-nature is originally without marks and yet not without marks, so whether there are marks or not need not be entertained in thought at all. This principle must not go unknown. Know that to entertain a thought is already discrimination, already clinging.

The doing away with marks has now been carried to its utmost point. This is also the place where everything since “no dharma resolves for bodhi” in the latter half is gathered into one conclusion. For at the very time of resolving, one must not grasp the dharma of bodhi, since the least grasping is clinging to marks of form. It is a chasing outward; it is not right knowledge and right view; it is attachment to dharmas and attachment to self; and it contradicts the nature that is empty and still. How then could one see the Tathāgata? This is why bodhisattvas are told to thoroughly understand the dharma of selflessness. Otherwise one practices blindly and drills in the dark, wanders onto a crooked path, and tries to cook sand into rice — one will never reach the goal. For cultivation has the seeing of the Tathāgata as its goal. Hence one should thoroughly understand.

Yet the doing away with marks means only that one must not grasp and cling. If one mistakes it for the annihilation of marks, that is again greatly wrong. Hence the next section follows. What comes below is (Zi) Second, the section “doing away with the annihilation of marks, to make clear that they are not different.” I shall first state its essential purport.

This section carries the weight of ten thousand jun not only within the latter half. Everything said since the opening of the sutra — that one should grasp neither non-dharmas nor non-non-dharmas, and the meanings of “is not” and “is called” — is only here explained as to why it is so. Hence, within the whole sutra, it is a critical juncture together with the preceding section on making clear that they are not one. It is like a thousand mountains and ten thousand ravines winding and meandering along; when the road reaches this point, they turn back, fold around, and gather into a single mass, so that the countless peaks and ridges that came before all catch one another’s light, each with its own feeling and momentum. You should know that the first half was spoken for those who were just beginning to resolve. Therefore both emptiness and existence are made ungraspable, so as to accord with the Middle Way. Wherever “is not” and “is called” are spoken, the tone for the most part attends to both sides: one must neither cling to existence nor cling to emptiness. What is called “is called” implies that although name and mark are provisional, they are not therefore nothing at all.

The latter half is spoken for those who have already brought forth the great resolve, cultivated the great practice, and can refrain from grasping any marks of dharmas. But it fears that they may grasp the dharma-marks of bodhi alone, and so remain burdened by emptiness and stillness and in the end fail to realize the nature. This clinging is exceedingly subtle and the hardest of all to remove. Therefore everything said in the latter half is directed at painfully doing away with the side of clinging to existence. Though at times “is not” and “is called” are spoken together, the tone mostly leans to the “is not” side, implying that though dharma-marks exist, they are in the end mere provisional names, and because they are provisional names, they are “not.” Only when one has done away with marks until not a speck of dust stains and not a thread hangs on does He then turn His head back and say that one should not cling to emptiness. Hence it is said to carry the weight of ten thousand jun. This is precisely what is meant by the saying in our school: “From the top of a hundred-foot pole, advance one step further.” It is also said: “You must still turn a somersault.” A somersault means turning the head around. Moreover, when the first half said one should not cling to emptiness, it stated only what is so; without the line here, “with respect to dharmas he does not speak of annihilation,” to awaken one, not only would the principle remain unclear and without conclusion, but the whole sutra’s spirit would not gather into one. Therefore the preceding section and this one are called the vital joints of the whole sutra, because they are where all the meanings spoken since the opening are gathered up. Nevertheless, once the latter half had opened, it was devoted to doing away with the clinging to existence. The preceding section, though it is the general conclusion of the doing away with existence and its meaning is deep and hidden, follows a single thread of principle and is still fairly easy to explain. But this section suddenly shifts its rudder and its gaze darts in all directions; its tone and spirit run straight through to the first half. Thus a single sentence embraces many meanings. Truly, viewed from the side it is a peak, viewed from the end it is a ridge — every face gives forth light, every face takes on a rare hue, and one does not know where to begin. To explain the principle face by face, it is best first to state its broad purport. Once the broad purport is clear, the several faces are also more easily clear.

You should know that the nature is the substance of all dharmas, while marks are the surface. Since the cultivator’s purpose is to realize the nature, he should not cling to the marks on the surface — this is a settled principle. Yet if there is an inside there must also be a face; if there were only a main structure and no surface at all, the main structure would stand alone and be of no use. Therefore one who cultivates in order to realize the nature should neither grasp marks nor annihilate marks — this too is a settled principle. Take house-building: the beams and pillars are the main frame, the substance; the doors, windows, walls, and even the bricks, tiles, lime, and stone are the surface, the marks. Naturally one attends first to the beams and pillars. If one knew only how to grasp the marks of the outer surface and did not know to attend to the substance of the main frame, how could that do? But if there were only the beams and pillars of the main frame and no doors, windows, or walls at all, could it still be called a house? House-building is like this, and cultivation is likewise. Seeing this parable, the principle that one should neither cling to marks nor abolish marks becomes clear. This is the most essential purport of the Buddha’s speaking this section.

blocks.text: Section Twenty-Seven: No Annihilation, No Extinction

inline.s: (Zi) Second, doing away with the annihilation of marks to make clear that they are not different. This has two parts: (Chou) first, pointing out and earnestly warning; next, concluding and revealing the right meaning.
(Chou) First, pointing out and earnestly warning.

“Subhūti, if you should have this thought: ‘The Tathāgata does not, by reason of the fully complete marks, attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi’ — Subhūti, do not have this thought: ‘The Tathāgata does not, by reason of the fully complete marks, attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”

From what has been said above, one can know how deep and broad is the meaning of this section on doing away with the annihilation of marks. Yet it is not only deep and broad. It also holds many hidden meanings, and its threads are many and tangled, so that it is extremely hard to explain. Since to explain is hard, one may know that to grasp it is hard. But since it is a vital juncture, one absolutely must grasp it with care. Take the opening of the first part, “pointing out and earnestly warning” — it is strange from the first word. What does it mean that the Tathāgata does not attain supreme bodhi by reason of the fully complete marks? You should know that on the surface it speaks of the fully complete marks, but in truth it hides the meaning of cultivating blessed merit, for the fully complete marks come from cultivating blessed merit. There are many sentence patterns of this kind in the Buddhist scriptures — what is called each mirroring the other. In plain words it could have said: do not have this thought, that the Tathāgata does not attain supreme bodhi by reason of cultivating blessed merit. Would that not be direct and to the point? That it does not say so but speaks instead of the fully complete marks contains two layers of deep meaning:

(1) To bring on the following passage, “he does not speak of the annihilation of marks,” so that, set against the earlier passage on not grasping marks, it makes clear the meaning of clinging to neither extreme. Moreover, “Tathāgata” is said above and “the fully complete marks” below, which reveals the meaning that although the nature is without marks, it is also not without marks.

(2) By saying “the fully complete marks,” the hearer can grasp that the sentence shadows forth the cultivation of blessed merit. Had it said “cultivating blessed merit,” the hearer might not have thought of the fully complete marks. This is what is called skillful speech. In sum, this double-edged way of speaking is used because the earlier passage said that the Wheel-Turning King too has the thirty-two marks and that they come from cultivating merit — which has already been refuted — and it was feared that people would mistakenly think one who realizes the nature need not cultivate merit. And because it was said above that to see me by form is to walk a crooked path, it was feared that people would mistakenly think one who would see the Tathāgata must annihilate marks. Speaking as He does here, both misunderstandings are dismissed; hence it is called skillful. In “if you should have this thought,” the word “this” refers to what follows, “does not by reason of the fully complete marks,” and so on. It is precisely because He fears that those who heard the earlier words might fall into misunderstanding and have this thought. The Elder is the one who fits the occasion, the representative of living beings, so He can only address Himself to the Elder; in truth it is a universal proclamation to all people.

The phrase “attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi” shadows forth many meanings and should be explained layer by layer. (1) Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi means supreme, universal, and right enlightenment. Yet it also includes the meanings of Buddha and Tathāgata. How does it include the meaning of Tathāgata? The Tathāgata is the equal Dharmakāya: there is no higher or lower, its substance is absolute and free of opposites, hence supreme; being equal, hence universal; without enlightenment one cannot realize it, hence right enlightenment. How does it include the meaning of the word Buddha? Buddha means awakened, hence right enlightenment; to awaken oneself and awaken others, with no duality or difference, hence universal; enlightenment already perfected, reaching the ultimate position, hence supreme. So “supreme, universal, and right enlightenment” may be called the collective name for the Tathāgata of intrinsic virtue and the Buddha of fruition-virtue. That here He says neither Buddha nor Tathāgata but raises the collective name is to reveal two meanings:

(A) Because the preceding clause openly speaks of the fully complete marks and hiddenly implies the cultivation of blessed merit. If it were spoken solely with respect to the blessed merit of cultivating the cause and attaining the fruit, the name Buddha should be used. If it were spoken solely with respect to the fully complete marks, which though not the nature are yet not apart from the nature, the name Tathāgata should be used. Since the preceding clause holds both the hidden and the open meanings, it is fitting to use the collective name that contains both the virtue of the nature and the virtue of the fruit.

(B) The single word “attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi” is precisely to bring on the following “resolves for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.” For it would use the fruition realized to make clear the causal mind. To use the fruit to make clear the cause is to elucidate the true meaning of what was said when the latter half opened: that in truth there is no dharma that resolves for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. At the opening it first stated the meaning that no dharma resolves for bodhi, then went on to make clear the meaning that no dharma attains bodhi — resolving and attaining spoken as a pair. Here likewise attaining and resolving are spoken as a pair, precisely to complete the meaning stated at the opening. What is meant by completing it? It elucidates that what was earlier called “dharma” includes non-dharma, and that what was earlier called “no dharma” means clinging to neither extreme — both dharma and non-dharma absent. Only thus is it resolving for bodhi. If one grasped only the one side of not grasping dharmas, one would inevitably fall into emptiness; could that still be called resolving for supreme bodhi? So here attaining and resolving are spoken together, and this is the essential purport that forms a delightful contrast with the opening’s speaking them together. From this it is further proved that since the earlier text has no word “mind” after bodhi, how could a word “mind” be attached here after “resolves for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi”? Those who do not understand the sutra’s purport have sloppily added one — is that not a great error?

(2) The single word “attains” has a further exquisite meaning. For this word “attains” is spoken precisely in contrast to the word “contemplate” of the preceding section. To speak of “attains” in contrast to “contemplate” is to make clear the meaning that in contemplating one should not grasp marks, while in attaining one should not abolish marks. Why? The way of cultivating contemplation puts its weight on seeing the nature; can the contemplation of marks see the nature? In the first half it was said plainly: “if one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.” Hence one who would see the Tathāgata must be able to see that all marks are precisely no marks, and only then. Now it says “contemplate the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks,” which has not yet seen marks as no marks — how could it see the Tathāgata? It wrongly cites the meaning of “such” and thinks itself right, not knowing that the meaning of “such” is that although marks are not abolished, one must also not grasp marks; only then is it named such. Now it clings to one side — how could that be named such? How muddled! Hence the rebuke: “he walks a crooked path and cannot see,” to make clear that nature and marks are not one.

This section does not speak of contemplation but of attainment, which is to speak with respect to cultivating the cause and realizing the fruit — that is, with respect to nature and marks attaining each other. Why? Because if nature and marks did not attain each other, it could not be called realizing the fruit. The sense is to show that if one can be unattached to marks, marks are after all no hindrance to the nature; hence they attain each other. In sum, the nature is the inside and marks are the outside. Spoken with respect to inside and outside, nature and marks are not one. Spoken with respect to the fact that where there is an outside there must be an inside, and where there is an inside there must be an outside — inside and outside united — nature and marks are not different. This is like one who would buy a house and should examine its beams and pillars. If he looked only at the outer appearance and said that looking at the outer appearance is looking at the beams and pillars, would that not be laughable? Yet if there were only the beams and pillars and no doors, windows, walls, or outer appearance at all, then even though he got the house, it would be as if he had not. Cultivation is likewise. Spoken with respect to contemplation, one must not grasp marks; spoken with respect to attainment, one must not abolish marks. Seeing this parable, the principle that neither oneness nor difference should be clung to should become thoroughly clear. One may further see that in all the Buddha’s Dharma-speaking, every phrase has its measure and every word contains a wondrous principle. It is truly feared that students, coarse of mind and flighty of temper, may swallow whole the principle that nature and marks are neither one nor different and fail to receive it quietly and in detail. Now, from what has been said above, our World-Honored One has painted, for all students, the sequential unfolding within the perfect fusion of nature and marks, clear and distinct. If one can profoundly comprehend it, one will naturally neither grasp marks nor grasp non-marks; one will have both the sequential unfolding and the perfect fusion; every matter will accord with the Middle Way, and every dharma will not go against the self-nature.

(3) What the preceding item said contains a further meaning of each mirroring the other, which must not go unknown. How so? The preceding section spoke of contemplation, which is spoken from the side of the cause, making clear that one who cultivates the cause must not grasp marks and must not cultivate defiled merit. You should know that if in cultivating the cause one must not grasp marks, how much less in realizing the fruit may one grasp marks — only one must not abolish marks. In the position of the cause one must not cultivate defiled merit, because only by cultivating an undefiled cause can one realize an undefiled fruit. This section speaks of attainment, which is spoken from the side of the fruit, making clear that one who realizes the fruit does not abolish marks, nor does he arrive there without cultivating merit. You should know that if realizing the fruit is not the abolition of marks, how could cultivating the cause be the abolition of marks? One must only not grasp and cling. The fruit is not arrived at without cultivating merit; therefore in the position of the cause one should only not cultivate defiled merit — who says one should cultivate absolutely none? Cause and fruit are of one suchness, and so each mirrors the other to make this clear.

(4) Viewed in contrast with each other, the preceding section and this one hold a further essential meaning. The sense of the prose in the preceding section is as if to say: the Wheel-Turning King too has the thirty-two marks and yet is not the Tathāgata — this makes clear the meaning that cultivating merit without cultivating wisdom cannot attain the fruit of supreme bodhi. This section earnestly warns against the thought of attaining bodhi without cultivating merit — this makes clear the meaning that cultivating wisdom without cultivating merit likewise cannot attain the fruit of supreme bodhi. In the four-line verse of the preceding section, the rebuke that to see the Tathāgata by form and sound is to walk a crooked path makes clear the meaning that one who would see the nature should not grasp marks. In this section, the earnest warning against the thought that the Tathāgata does not attain bodhi by the fully complete marks makes clear the meaning that seeing the nature is also not the abolition of marks. From the first item to this fourth, viewed together, they have spoken of principle, nature, event, and cultivation, and of the causes and fruits of nature and marks being neither one nor different, both sequentially unfolded and perfectly fused, with the utmost fineness and detail, the utmost completeness. Yet the meaning they contain does not stop even here.

(5) The preceding section says “contemplate,” and this section says “thought.” To contemplate and to think are one meaning. Taken together, the two sections show that to cling to neither extreme — neither marks nor non-marks, neither merit nor non-merit — is right contemplation and right thought. If one grasps only one side, it is not right contemplation or right thought. Why? Because it does not accord with the Middle Way. Therefore in the preceding section, grasping marks is rebuked as walking a crooked path; and in this section, grasping non-marks is earnestly warned against with “do not have this thought.”

(6) The thirty-two marks belong to the response body, and the response body is subject to birth and death and impermanence, which suits making clear that nature and marks are not one. Hence when the preceding section did away with the grasping of marks, it brought up the thirty-two marks. The fully complete marks are what was earlier called the fully complete marks; they are the reward body. Yet spoken with respect to marks it is named the reward body; spoken with respect to the nature it is the Dharmakāya obtained as reward — which suits making clear that nature and marks are not different. Hence when this section does away with the annihilation of marks, it brings up the fully complete marks. You should know that speaking thus is also a case of each mirroring the other to make the meaning clear. Why? Since the thirty-two marks should not be grasped, one may know that the fully complete marks should not be grasped either. Since the fully complete marks should not be annihilated, one may know that the thirty-two marks should not be annihilated either. That they are spoken of separately is only for the convenience of making clear the meaning that they are neither one nor different.

(7) In “does not attain bodhi by the fully complete marks” there is a further exquisite meaning. You should know that the accomplishment of the fully complete marks comes from cultivating both merit and wisdom, not from cultivating merit alone. What is meant by cultivating both? At the very time of cultivating merit, one knows not to cling to marks — and to know not to cling to marks is wisdom. For this reason one can accomplish the fully complete marks and attain supreme bodhi. This differs greatly in tenor from the Wheel-Turning King, for the Wheel-Turning King’s karma of merit is called defiled for no other reason than that he cultivates merit while clinging to marks. Hence he can only accomplish the thirty-two marks and can only attain the fruit of a Wheel-Turning King. From this one may know that although this section speaks of not annihilating marks, it in fact also contains the meaning of not grasping marks. This is why it can be not different from the nature. This layer is the exquisite meaning of this section. The purpose of bringing up the fully complete marks to make clear that they are not different lies here. Why? Not being different is one suchness; only when one grasps neither of the two extremes, marks and non-marks, can it be called one suchness. If, as in the preceding section, one knew only not to grasp the one side of non-marks, how could that be called one suchness?

Gathering all the meanings spoken above, the meaning of this section can be seen through. It is nothing but the fear that people, hearing the earlier teaching on doing away with marks, might lean to the side of emptiness and mistakenly think it absolute marklessness, which would contradict the true marks that are neither with marks nor without marks. Then it would not be the meaning of all dharmas being such, nor the equality of all dharmas, and one would not attain the fruit of supreme bodhi nor see the Tathāgata. Hence the earnest warning, “do not have this thought.” For to have this thought is a wrong view, not a right view. In reason and in tone, the single sentence “do not have this thought” is already sufficient in meaning. That He goes on to say the two clauses “the Tathāgata does not by reason of the fully complete marks” is to repeat it in order to make it plain, so that people may know that attending to these two clauses is essential and not to be slighted. Therefore “do not have this thought” must be read in one breath together with the two clauses that follow. If one breaks the sentence at the word “thought,” the two clauses below will seem redundant.

I have seen an early Qing printing that mistakenly broke the sentence at the word “thought.” Then, finding the two clauses below redundant, it deleted the word “not,” making it read: “The Tathāgata, by reason of the fully complete marks, attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.” This is a great error. You should know that the presence of the word “not” contains the meaning that although one should not grasp marks, one should also not abolish marks; the tone then illumines both extremes, how perfectly fused and alive. If the word “not” is deleted, the tone clings to the one side of grasping marks, sticky and dull, a world apart. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: prajñā is like a great mass of fire, untouchable from any side. How could one blunt a single phrase? Look at the wording of this sutra: not one word is spoken to a dead end. As writing, it is a stroke of divine inspiration. Without Master Kumārajīva’s translating hand, it could not be so wondrous. Take other translations and compare them, and you will know. It is fortunate that other printings did not imitate this early Qing printing; otherwise the current circulating edition would have one more poison in it.
(Chou) Second, concluding and revealing the right meaning.

“Subhūti, if you should have this thought: ‘One who resolves for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi speaks of all dharmas as annihilated’ — do not have this thought. Why? One who resolves for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi does not, with respect to dharmas, speak of the mark of annihilation.”

The meaning of the sutra in this section is most winding and minute; one should receive it with a quiet mind. In the current circulating edition there is a word “mind” after bodhi; the Tang-dynasty manuscript sutras all lack it. The addition of the word “mind” probably began in the Five Dynasties period and should not be made.

This section precisely explains the reason for the preceding section of pointing out and earnestly warning. The passage from “if you should have this thought” down to “speaks of all dharmas as annihilated” explains the reason for the earlier having of this thought. The passage after “why” explains the reason for the earlier “do not have this thought.” The right meaning of the preceding section is only revealed here; hence the section is headed “concluding and revealing the right meaning.” “If you should have this thought” means having the thought that the Tathāgata does not, by reason of the fully complete marks, attain supreme bodhi.

The word “dharmas” in “speaks of all dharmas” follows closely upon the fully complete marks. For the fully complete marks are accomplished by cultivating merit, and what is cultivating merit but widely practicing the six pāramitās and all such dharmas? Therefore to say “not by the fully complete marks” is no different from saying one need not practice the six pāramitās. Would that not be speaking of all dharmas as annihilated? Hence “speaks of all dharmas as annihilated.” Why does the phrase “resolves for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi” stand in between? You should know that when the latter half opened, the World-Honored One had said that no dharma resolves for bodhi. It was truly feared that those who could not deeply grasp its meaning, hearing Him later say again, “with respect to anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, there is not even the least dharma to be attained,” and hearing the preceding section say, “if one sees me by form, that is a crooked path, and one cannot see the Tathāgata,” would inevitably misunderstand and say: the earlier meaning that no dharma resolves for bodhi, I understand. Since one who attains bodhi has not the least dharma, and since it is plainly taught that seeing by form is a crooked path — and form means marks — it is evident that the Tathāgata’s attainment of supreme bodhi has nothing at all to do with the fully complete marks. This is the origin of the thought that He does not attain bodhi by reason of the fully complete marks. Having this thought, one then has a second thought: the fully complete marks come from practicing the six pāramitās and diligently cultivating merit — what is called cultivating marks and excellences for a hundred kalpas. Now since attaining bodhi has nothing to do with the fully complete marks, and since it is plainly taught that one who attains bodhi has not the least dharma, it is evident that one who resolves for bodhi likewise must have not the least dharma; one need only turn the mind single-mindedly toward the nature that is empty and still. All the six pāramitās and such dharmas, the cultivating of merit and of marks and excellences, must not be kept in mind at all. This is why it was taught that no dharma resolves for bodhi. If a practitioner misunderstands in this way, he runs counter to the Buddha’s intent, walks onto a crooked path, and will inevitably cultivate not a single dharma. Why? Because he has spoken of all dharmas as annihilated. Could that still be called resolving for supreme bodhi? Hence the earnest warning, “do not have this thought.”

From this one may know that the Buddha’s speaking this section is precisely an explanation of why one might have this thought. And that the Buddha, at the moment of doing away with the grasping of marks, suddenly turned His head back and spoke this whole section on doing away with the annihilation of marks, is precisely an elucidation of the true meaning of the earlier saying that no dharma resolves for bodhi. The importance of this section’s bearing is clear. Hence I said a moment ago that its meaning is most winding and minute, and that one should receive it with a quiet mind. Whenever principle is expounded to its subtle depths, one must examine it closely; otherwise one will inevitably diverge by a hair and err by a thousand miles, walk onto a crooked path without knowing it — the utmost danger. This is why a student of Buddhism should open a perfect understanding, and why drawing near to a good teacher is an urgent matter.

What follows “why” precisely makes clear the reason one should not have this thought. The sense is as if to say: the earlier statement that no dharma resolves for bodhi means that one should not harbor the thought, “this is supreme bodhi,” in order to cure the disease of grasping dharma-marks. When did it ever say that dharma-marks are annihilated? Hence: one who resolves for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi does not, with respect to dharmas, speak of the mark of annihilation. When it was earlier said that no dharma resolves for bodhi, it was already said plainly: one who resolves for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi need only bring forth the mind that takes on the duty of saving living beings, which duty he ought to fulfill, and that even in fulfilling it is as though not fulfilling it. How could that be speaking of annihilating all dharmas? And when it was later said that if a bodhisattva says, “I should save countless living beings to nirvāṇa,” then he is not named a bodhisattva, this too means that one must not harbor the thought that one is able to fulfill the duty. How could that be speaking of annihilating all dharmas? That the Buddha attained bodhi with not the least dharma to be attained means that although He attained it, He did not harbor the thought of having attained — it is not the annihilation of all dharmas either. To realize the Dharmakāya and attain bodhi, one must cultivate both merit and wisdom, since only by cultivating both are compassion and wisdom complete. How could one say that the fully complete marks are absolutely irrelevant? To misunderstand in such a way is a great, great error. You should know that the World-Honored One, in His great compassion, because He had just now done away with marks to the utmost, feared that the muddle-headed, unable to grasp it deeply, could hardly avoid this misunderstanding; hence He warned so earnestly. Such a warning is not only to elucidate the true meaning of no dharma resolving for bodhi; it is also meant to teach students that one who would realize the equal Dharmakāya and the meaning of all dharmas being such must put the mad mind entirely to rest and bring not a single thought into being — only then is it possible. Why? Because the moment a thought stirs there is discrimination and clinging. Hence “do not have this thought.” From this it is plainly evident that here, after the word bodhi, no word “mind” can possibly be attached.

In sum: had there not been these two large sections under “separately doing away with the clinging of feeling,” the various meanings spoken since the sutra’s opening would be hard to grasp thoroughly, and there would be no way to expound them. You should know that all the ways of speaking from the sutra’s opening, expounding the principle of doing away with both extremes, are spoken by gathering in the meaning of these two large sections. Hence these two large sections are a vital juncture of the whole sutra, because their meaning can run through the entire sutra.

Take the first half, which says at the outset: “I shall save countless, numberless, boundless living beings to nirvāṇa, and yet in truth there is no living being who attains nirvāṇa.” This means saving all living beings without clinging to marks; it does not mean not saving a single being and so making the mark of annihilation. Again it says: “with respect to dharmas one should dwell on nothing and practice giving.” This means that when practicing giving one should not dwell on marks; it does not mean not practicing giving and so making the mark of annihilation. What is called “thus should one subdue” means that both extremes, clinging and annihilation, must be subdued — not one side subdued. What is called “he should only abide as taught” means that both extremes are subdued and neither extreme is dwelt in. Dwelling thus on nothing, one naturally attains what one should abide in; and that is abiding as taught. Hence: “if the mind has abiding, then it is non-abiding.” That the World-Honored One showed Himself as sharing the toil-dusted marks of ordinary beings is precisely a demonstration of not clinging to the fully complete marks or the thirty-two marks, while yet not annihilating marks. This is what is called one suchness, what is called equality. That is why this sutra has boundless merit, and one whose faith is not contrary will bear the Tathāgata’s burden, increase merit, extinguish offenses, and surely attain bodhi. Yet this meaning is most profound and must be deeply grasped; otherwise one will either be terrified and doubt, or muddled and deranged.

Nor is that all. The earlier phrase “thoroughly understands the dharma of selflessness” means that one should thoroughly understand not only the principle of not grasping dharma-marks, but also the principle of not annihilating dharma-marks. Why? If one grasps dharma-marks, one clings to self, person, being, and life. If one grasps non-dharma-marks, one likewise clings to self, person, being, and life. Only when with respect to all dharma-marks one neither grasps nor annihilates can one realize the dharma-nature of equal one suchness and be without self. That is truly to have thoroughly understood. Hence, having gained these two large sections, the whole sutra melts into one piece, and its meaning is fully proclaimed. That is why the next section completes the conclusion with “understands that all dharmas are without self and attains accomplishment in patience.”

In these two large sections making clear that they are neither one nor different, there is a further most essential meaning. What is it? It is what is called neither permanent nor annihilated. The section making clear that they are not one speaks of impermanence: the response-transformation body of the thirty-two marks appears from time to time and is subject to birth and death, hence impermanent; and because it is impermanent, it is not one with the permanently abiding nature. The section making clear that they are not different speaks of non-annihilation: the fully complete marks are the Dharmakāya obtained as reward, hence not annihilated; and because not annihilated, they are not different from the permanently abiding nature. Nevertheless, this is still spoken according to a provisional meaning. If one speaks according to the ultimate, definitive meaning, then all three bodies — Dharma, reward, and response — are neither permanent nor annihilated. In these two large sections, “Tathāgata” is plainly said, which refers to the Dharmakāya; “the fully complete marks” is plainly said, which refers to the reward body; “the thirty-two marks” is plainly said, which refers to the response body. Now the three bodies are spoken of together to make clear that one should not grasp marks and should not annihilate marks — because they are impermanent, one should not grasp them; because they are not annihilated, one should not annihilate them. From this one may see that the sutra’s purport plainly reveals the meaning that the three bodies are neither permanent nor annihilated. How could that be omitted and left unspoken? This meaning is likewise an essential purport of prajñā and must not go unknown. Why? When the meaning of neither permanent nor annihilated is clear, the meaning of neither one nor different becomes clearer still; and when the meaning of neither one nor different is seen through, then one’s view is perfect and one’s knowledge is right. Yet this meaning is by no means easy to make clear. Among the great Vehicle sutras and treatises, though it is spoken of again and again, none sets it forth more fully and penetratingly than the ten-fascicle Golden Light Sutra. I shall now quote and expound it, which I imagine you would all wish to hear.

That sutra says: ‘Depending on this Dharmakāya, the inconceivable mahā-samādhi becomes manifest. Depending on this Dharmakāya, all great wisdom becomes manifest. Therefore the two bodies become manifest depending on samādhi and depending on wisdom.’ Mahā means great. Samādhi means concentration. Great concentration is spoken in contrast to great wisdom; great wisdom is great insight. Concentration and wisdom become manifest from the absolute Dharmakāya, hence both are called great. That both are called great makes clear the equality of concentration and wisdom. Making clear the equality of concentration and wisdom reveals the simultaneity of stillness and illumination. Concentration and wisdom are spoken with respect to the work of cultivation; stillness and illumination are spoken with respect to what the nature intrinsically possesses. In stillness there is illumination, in illumination there is stillness — beyond what words or thought can reach, what is called being apart from names and cut off from marks. Hence “inconceivable.” This sentence governs “all great wisdom” as well.

The two bodies are the reward body and the response body. The sense is that the nature-substance of the Dharmakāya is originally apart from names and cut off from marks, with stillness and illumination simultaneous; but without cultivation it cannot be realized. Yet if the nature-substance did not intrinsically possess them, the work of cultivating concentration and wisdom could likewise not manifest them. Hence: depending on this Dharmakāya, great concentration and great wisdom become manifest — this is the surface meaning. Underneath, it teaches that one must be apart from names and cut off from marks, cultivating concentration in reliance on the intrinsic stillness and cultivating wisdom in reliance on the intrinsic illumination. When the work of cultivating concentration and wisdom is complete and equal, one can have stillness and illumination simultaneous, which is to realize the Dharmakāya. Once the Dharmakāya is realized, the marks of the two bodies, reward and response, appear again. Hence: therefore the two bodies become manifest depending on samādhi and wisdom. Seeing the meaning of this passage, one may know that one must be apart from names and cut off from marks in order to cultivate concentration and wisdom, and only thus can one realize the nature of the Dharmakāya. Yet one does not thereby annihilate the marks of the two bodies, reward and response. In that sutra the names of the two bodies are slightly different: what is commonly called the reward body it renders as the response body, and what is commonly called the response body it renders as the transformation body. In all the sutras, treatises, and the writings of the ancient worthies, such variant names are met with constantly, and beginners often find them distressing. Yet if one looks carefully at the sutra’s purport, one knows what is meant and can reconcile them; there is no need to dread the difficulty.

That sutra also says: ‘Thus the Dharmakāya, samādhi, and wisdom pass beyond all marks, are unattached to marks, are beyond discrimination, and are neither permanent nor annihilated — this is named the Middle Way.’ This makes clear that the Dharmakāya is neither permanent nor annihilated. “The Dharmakāya, samādhi, and wisdom” is meant to show that concentration and wisdom complete and full are the Dharmakāya; there is no separate Dharmakāya apart from these. For samādhi and wisdom refer precisely to the Dharmakāya. One must not mistakenly take Dharmakāya, samādhi, and wisdom as three separate things. Looking at the passage quoted above from that sutra, “depending on this Dharmakāya,” and so forth, this becomes clear. Why? It has always been said that the reward body and the response body appear from the Dharmakāya, whereas that sutra says the two bodies become manifest depending on samādhi and wisdom — ample proof that samādhi and wisdom are the Dharmakāya. That is why the intrinsic nature of ordinary beings is called only Buddha-nature; sometimes it is called the Dharmakāya wrapped in defilement, or the Dharmakāya obstructed, but it is never simply called the Dharmakāya. Precisely because they have no concentration and wisdom, or have them but not in full. Since they have not realized the one true dharma-realm and cannot have stillness and illumination simultaneous, how could it be called the Dharmakāya? Since, then, concentration and wisdom must be complete for it to be named the Dharmakāya, it is evident that the Dharmakāya is nothing other than the completeness of concentration and wisdom.

The four phrases beginning with “pass beyond all marks” make the meaning clear with the utmost refinement. “Pass beyond” means to transcend. “Pass beyond all marks” is like saying, to be beyond marks. Since it has already said “pass beyond all marks,” why does it go on to say “unattached to marks”? The phrase “pass beyond all marks” makes clear that it is without marks: the nature-substance is great with nothing outside it and small with nothing inside it, standing aloof beyond all opposites, and so is without marks.

The phrase “unattached to marks” makes clear that it is not without marks; because it is not without marks, there can be talk of non-attachment. For although the nature is not marks, all marks appear from the nature. Though they appear from the nature, the nature still stands beyond them, and so is unattached. These two phrases illuminate each other’s meaning: because it is aloof, it is unattached; because it is unattached, one knows it is aloof. The meaning of the two phrases joined is precisely to reveal that nature and marks are not one. Why? Because although the nature follows conditions and manifests marks, it still remains aloof and unattached. The non-attachment spoken of here means that it is spontaneously, by its very nature, unattached. How is this seen? Marks are all subject to birth and death and impermanence, while the nature abides permanently as ever, and is not obstructed by these birth-and-death marks merely because it follows conditions and manifests marks. So one may know that it was unattached from the first. Hence nature and marks are not one. These two phrases also explain that the Dharmakāya and the two bodies, reward and response, are not one.

The phrase “beyond discrimination” serves to reveal that nature and marks are not different — that is, that the Dharmakāya and the two bodies, reward and response, are not different. Why is it that being beyond discrimination means not being different? That sutra itself makes its meaning clear: ‘Though there is discrimination, the substance is without discrimination. Though the number is three, it is not three substances.’ The sense is that the two bodies, reward and response, have only marks and no substance; the substance is the Dharmakāya alone. Hence though the number is three, the substance is not three; though the marks differ, the substance does not differ. So the words “beyond discrimination” are spoken with respect to the substance. Yet they are also double-edged: because it manifests marks of discrimination at every moment, there can be talk of being beyond discrimination. Thus the phrase “beyond discrimination,” on the one hand, reveals that its substance has no difference, while on the other hand it reveals that its manifestation of marks never ceases. From this one may know the boundary between not one and not different. For when the nature melts marks into itself, they are not different; when nature and marks are set over against each other, they are not one.

“Neither permanent nor annihilated” follows closely upon the three preceding phrases. Because at every moment it manifests marks whose substance, though undifferentiated, is differentiated in function, it is said to be impermanent. Yet though the marks are impermanent, the nature of the Dharmakāya still passes beyond all marks and is unattached to marks, and so it is said to be not annihilated.

Someone may ask: it has always been said that the Dharmakāya is permanent; because it is permanent it is named the Dharmakāya. So to say the Dharmakāya is not annihilated is easy to understand. Though the Dharmakāya manifests the marks of reward and response and so on, the present statement that it is impermanent is likewise spoken with respect to marks. But then why say the Dharmakāya is impermanent? This meaning is after all hard to make clear. Answer: what is called the permanence of the Dharmakāya is spoken with respect to the Dharmakāya alone. Yet once one has realized the permanently abiding, non-arising, non-ceasing substance of the Dharmakāya, if one dwelt in the substance and never manifested marks, one could not come near living beings — how then could one benefit them? Therefore all Buddhas and all great bodhisattvas, for the sake of benefiting all living beings, constantly manifest the birth-and-death marks of the reward body and the response-transformation bodies and so on, without dwelling and clinging to the Dharmakāya. With respect to the fact that they possess a permanently abiding Dharmakāya and yet do not dwell in it, it is said that the Dharmakāya is impermanent. Yet although they do not dwell in it, because they are constantly within the great concentration, the marks they manifest, however blazingly subject to birth and death, leave the Dharmakāya’s permanence as it was. What is called passing beyond all marks and being unattached to marks truly comes from this. Hence it is also said that the Dharmakāya is not annihilated. You should know that the Dharmakāya’s impermanence is precisely what is called not dwelling in nirvāṇa, and the Dharmakāya’s non-annihilation is precisely what is called not dwelling in birth and death. Dwelling in neither extreme, it is named the Middle Way. That the Dharmakāya dwells in neither extreme means that it clings neither to the Dharmakāya nor to the marks of reward and response and so on. This is precisely the state of stillness and illumination simultaneous. Unless the work of concentration and wisdom is cultivated to completeness and equality, one cannot reach this state. That this sutra at its opening bids one make the great vow, cultivate the great practice, and remove self-clinging is for this reason. For while self-clinging is unconverted, there must be discrimination and clinging; with the least discrimination and clinging, one cannot dwell in neither extreme, and how then could concentration and wisdom be equal? How then could the state of stillness and illumination simultaneous ever be reached?

That sutra further says: ‘As for the transformation body: it constantly turns the wheel of Dharma, everywhere following conditions, and its skillful continuity is unbroken; therefore it is said to be permanent. Because it is not the root, and because its fully complete great function does not appear, it is said to be impermanent.’ That sutra renders the response body as the transformation body. This makes clear that the response body is neither permanent nor annihilated. “Therefore it is said to be permanent” is like saying, therefore it is said to be not annihilated: because the response body follows conditions and manifests unceasingly, it is said to be not annihilated. “Impermanent” is like saying not permanent. “Because it is not the root” means that the response body is not the substance of the intrinsic nature. The bodies of reward and response and so on are all manifested marks and functions of the intrinsic nature, and so are not the root. Function is manifested from the root; the root is not manifested from function. The two bodies, reward and response, are already function and cannot manifest a further function; hence “its fully complete great function does not appear.” This phrase precisely makes clear that reward and response are marks. Marks are dharmas of birth and death, and so are said to be impermanent.

That sutra also says: ‘As for the response body: from beginningless time it continues unbroken; because it can gather and uphold the dharmas not shared in common by all Buddhas, and because living beings are endless and its function is likewise endless, it is said to be permanent. Because it is not the root, and because its fully complete function does not appear, it is said to be impermanent.’ This makes clear that the reward body is neither permanent nor annihilated — for that sutra renders the reward body as the response body. The dharmas not shared in common, such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, are possessed by Buddhas alone; bodhisattvas too do not have them in full, hence “not shared in common.” “Gather and uphold” has two senses. First, these dharmas not shared in common are the wisdom-function of the reward body and are gathered and upheld within the reward body. Second, because the reward body possesses this wisdom-function, it can in turn gather and uphold living beings. Hence it continues: living beings are endless and its function is likewise endless. Gathering the meaning of the passages quoted above, we find that the neither-one-nor-different has three senses.

The Dharmakāya is substance; the bodies of reward and response and so on are function. Hence they are not one. If substance gathers function into itself, they are beyond discrimination; hence they are not different. This is the first sense.

Now the Dharmakāya’s impermanence is a permanence that is impermanent; the two bodies’ non-annihilation is an annihilation that is not annihilated. Hence the Dharmakāya’s impermanence is the two bodies’ non-annihilation; this is why nature and marks are not different. The Dharmakāya’s non-annihilation is ultimately not annihilated; the two bodies’ impermanence is ultimately impermanent. Hence the Dharmakāya’s non-annihilation is the two bodies’ impermanence; this is why nature and marks are not one. How so? The Dharmakāya’s impermanence is spoken with respect to its continuously manifesting marks. When the sutra says “beyond discrimination,” it makes clear that though it continuously manifests marks, the substance is the Dharmakāya alone. Because it continuously manifests marks, it is said to be impermanent; because the substance is the Dharmakāya alone, it is said to be a permanence that is impermanent. The Dharmakāya’s non-annihilation is spoken with respect to the permanently abiding substance itself. When the sutra says “passes beyond all marks, unattached to marks,” this precisely makes clear its permanently abiding substance. Because its substance permanently abides, it can manifest marks and yet remain aloof and unattached. Because the substance permanently abides, it is said to be not annihilated; because it manifests marks and yet remains aloof and unattached, it is said that its non-annihilation is ultimately not annihilated. The two bodies are not so. The two bodies’ impermanence is spoken with respect to their not being the substance itself; the sutra says, “because it is not the root.” Since they are not the substance, it is said that their impermanence is ultimately impermanent. Hence the Dharmakāya’s non-annihilation is the two bodies’ impermanence; this is why nature and marks are not one. Why? Because the one permanently abides as substance, while the other is not the substance. The two bodies’ non-annihilation is spoken with respect to the continuity of their manifesting marks; the sutra says, “because it continues unbroken.” Since they manifest in continuity, it is said to be not annihilated. Hence the Dharmakāya’s impermanence is the two bodies’ non-annihilation; this is why nature and marks are not different. Why? Because both are spoken with respect to the continuity of manifesting marks. This is another sense of the neither-one-nor-different.

Furthermore, the name “neither permanent nor annihilated” as applied to the three bodies is not different; yet the reason why the Dharmakāya is neither permanent nor annihilated and the reason why the two bodies are neither permanent nor annihilated are not one. This is yet another sense of the neither-one-nor-different.

In sum, when one speaks of oneness there are various kinds of oneness, and when one speaks of difference there are various kinds of difference. Moreover, within oneness there is difference, and within difference there is oneness. Therefore to speak of oneness or difference is wrong, and to speak of neither oneness nor difference is also wrong; to speak of oneness or difference is right, and to speak of neither oneness nor difference is also right. Thus it is neither speakable nor unspeakable: cling, and all are wrong; do not cling, and all are right. One should see thus, one should know thus. To see thus is perfect seeing; to know thus is right knowledge.

Someone may ask: from the sutra passages quoted above, one can see that the two bodies, reward and response, are alike marks of birth and death and alike not the root. Why then does this sutra make clear the not-one with respect to the response body and the not-different with respect to the reward body? You should know that the continuity of the response-transformation body is manifested by skillful means, following conditions, after the Dharmakāya has been realized — and the Wheel-Turning King has it too, whereas the nature-substance of the Dharmakāya permanently abides without change. Its not being one is most evident. Hence the thirty-two marks of the response-transformation are used to make clear the not-one.

As for the reward body, it is accomplished simultaneously with the Dharmakāya. Hence this sutra says: “by reason of the fully complete marks he attains supreme bodhi,” which precisely makes clear that accomplishing the fully complete marks is realizing supreme bodhi. One should note the word “by reason of.” Again, when the Golden Light Sutra makes clear the meaning of the reward body, it says: ‘As for the response body (that is, the reward body), from beginningless time it continues unbroken.’ The phrase “continues unbroken” is common to reward and response; this makes clear that they are not one with the Dharmakāya. The phrase “from beginningless time” belongs to the reward body alone; this makes clear that it is not different from the Dharmakāya. You should know that the Dharmakāya may be called beginningless, whereas the reward body is only realized after ignorance is exhausted. Why then does it say “from beginningless time”? This meaning is most refined and becomes clear only when carefully dissected.

For the reward body has two names: one is the reward body for one’s own enjoyment, the other the reward body for others’ enjoyment. This sutra’s “the fully complete marks,” and the Golden Light Sutra’s “continues unbroken,” “living beings are endless and its function is likewise endless,” are all spoken with respect to the enjoyment of others. Yet only when the meaning of one’s own enjoyment is clear does the meaning of others’ enjoyment become clear.

Let me first speak of one’s own enjoyment. The reward body for one’s own enjoyment is nothing else: it refers to the perfect wisdom inwardly realized for one’s own benefit, and is only provisionally named a body. This wisdom certainly appears through the work of cultivation, yet it is intrinsically possessed by the nature-substance. If it were not intrinsically possessed, cultivation would not manifest it either — just as boring water cannot bring forth fire, and boiling sand cannot make rice. Since the nature-substance is beginningless, this wisdom too is beginningless. Hence the reward body for one’s own enjoyment is beginningless.

Now let me speak with respect to others’ enjoyment. One’s own enjoyment and others’ enjoyment, though the names are two, are in fact one. Spoken with respect to the perfect wisdom inwardly realized for one’s own benefit, it is called one’s own enjoyment; spoken with respect to the great function of manifesting marks to benefit others, it is called others’ enjoyment. Since it is called perfect wisdom, there must be a great function; without a great function, how could it be called perfect wisdom? One is the surface and one the inside, and they seem to be two; yet only when surface and inside are united does it receive the name of a body. Hence the names are two but the reality is one. Moreover, wisdom is intrinsically possessed, and function too is intrinsically possessed. Therefore the reward body for others’ enjoyment is likewise beginningless. Gathering all these meanings, the fact that the reward body is not different from the Dharmakāya is evident. Hence the fully complete marks of the reward body are used to make clear the not-different. If one speaks in strict truth, even the response-transformation body may be called beginningless. How so? The response-transformation body is the matter of cultivating all kinds of dharmas and penetrating conventional truth; when the practice is complete, one attains great freedom and can therefore manifest all kinds of bodies according to the minds of living beings. But how does one penetrate the matters of conventional truth? Through the wisdom that penetrates ultimate truth. So one may see that matters are gathered into wisdom. Hence if the reward body is beginningless, the response body is beginningless too. Why then is the response body alone used to make clear the not-one? Because the reward body is intimate with the Dharmakāya, while the response body is comparatively distant. What is meant by intimate? Others’ enjoyment is the manifested marks and function, the surface; one’s own enjoyment is the intrinsically possessed wisdom, the inside. Yet the manifestation of marks and function is manifested precisely in wisdom, and the possession of wisdom is possessed precisely in the principle-substance. Moreover, principle and wisdom are one suchness, with no division of possessor and possessed, no distinction of manifester and manifested. Therefore, whether one’s own or others’ enjoyment, it is truly fused into one with the principle-substance — hence intimate, and being intimate, not different. What is meant by distant? Although the response-transformation body is likewise possessed in principle and wisdom, with no such distinctions of possessor and possessed or manifester and manifested, yet it belongs exclusively to the outwardly manifested marks, and so is distant; being distant, it is not one.

Look at what the Golden Light Sutra says, and it becomes clear. In making clear the meaning of the reward body, it says both “beginningless” and “gathers and upholds the dharmas not shared in common.” To bring up the inner upholding is precisely to make clear its intimacy with the Dharmakāya. In making clear the meaning of the response-transformation, it says “everywhere following conditions by skillful means.” To bring up the outer following is precisely to make clear its distance from the Dharmakāya. In sum, when the meaning of neither permanent nor annihilated is clear, then the meaning of neither one nor different is thoroughly clear; and the meanings of all dharmas being one suchness and all dharmas being equal are thoroughly clear as well. Why? Because the three bodies are all neither permanent nor annihilated and are not different, hence one suchness. Yet their being neither permanent nor annihilated differs in each case and so they are not one; hence although there is one suchness, it does not hinder the existence of all dharmas. Moreover, within oneness there is difference and within difference there is oneness. Therefore difference is difference appearing within equality, and equality is equality appearing within difference. They neither block each other nor confuse each other. Sequential unfolding does not obstruct perfect fusion, and perfect fusion does not obstruct sequential unfolding. This is what is called perfect middle. Negation and illumination simultaneous, dissolving and sustaining at ease — how could it be merely that one clings to neither extreme? And the essential work of cultivation lies only in not grasping marks, not annihilating marks, and taking the nature as the pivot. Once one has realized the substance of the nature that is empty and still, then by the power of permeation one likewise neither grasps nor annihilates, responding to opportunities and following conditions, with a great function that never ends. Not only does one not dwell in marks — one does not dwell in the nature either, and does not dwell even in non-dwelling. Yet the pivot of the great mirror wisdom remains as it was. This is what is called attaining supreme bodhi by cultivating all good dharmas with no self, person, and so on. This is what is called the Diamond Prajñā Pāramitā, by which the Buddha’s mind-seal is transmitted. To penetrate this principle and recite the Buddha’s name is to attain the one-mind of principle and surely be born in the Pure Land of Permanent Tranquil Light. I would share this encouragement with you all.
(Ren) Third, concluding selflessness with respect to not receiving blessed merit.

The meaning of the word yue in this section’s heading is that everything is without self, and here the one dharma of not receiving blessed merit is merely used to make that meaning clear. The principles spoken above — no holy, no ordinary; neither one nor different — likewise hold for every dharma, but they were spoken with respect to saving living beings and to nature and marks because those are easier to grasp. The word yue is like the ordinary word jiu, “with respect to.” The Buddhist scriptures prefer yue to jiu because jiu is shallow while yue is deep and refined. Yue carries the sense of “roughly”: it shows that one matter is provisionally taken as an example, without going on to explain each in detail. Yue also carries the sense of “binding”: as a net has its main rope, and lifting the main rope brings the whole net into order, it shows that although only this one matter is spoken of, the main rope is already grasped and the rest may be inferred. Yue also carries the sense of “covenant”: like a contract, which after long time is not forgotten, it shows that the meaning made clear here fits most exactly, and can be trusted without error. Were the word jiu used, none of these three senses would be present. Some have doubted that yue is recondite and thought jiu more common; let me take this occasion to say a word about it. The sayings of the ancient worthies before the Tang are not for later students to criticize lightly. That no other matter is taken up, but only not receiving blessed merit, follows from the text above. The fully complete marks above shadow forth the cultivation of blessed merit, making clear that one who attains the supreme fruit does not abolish the cultivation of merit. This section follows closely on that meaning and elucidates it, saying: how could the cultivation of merit be abolished? One need only not receive and not cling. And it adds, by way of completion: one must not, hearing that the cultivation of merit is not abolished, thereupon give rise to greed and clinging. Hence with this section, the meaning of the preceding section becomes more complete and perfect. This is what is called the text not joining but the meaning joining.

blocks.text: Section Twenty-Eight: Not Receiving and Not Coveting

inline.s: (Ren) This section has two parts: (Gui) first, concluding selflessness; next, making clear non-attachment. (Gui) first has two parts: (Zi) first, making clear the superiority of the merit of selflessness; next, making clear that it comes from not receiving. (Zi) first has two parts: (Chou) first, citing the case; next, comparing the superiority.
(Chou) First, citing the case.
“Subhūti, if a bodhisattva gives in charity the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges …”

The current circulating edition reads “takes and uses them for giving.” Liu’s text and Hui’s edition lack the words “takes and uses.” Giving the seven treasures already contains the sense of taking and using them.

In the latter half there are only one or two places that compare and reveal the sutra’s merit; and even there the intent is not the comparison, which is only borrowed for another use. First, it serves to make a division. Second, it serves to make some other meaning clear. Thus here, the merit of giving is borrowed to show that one who has accomplished non-receiving has attained the patience of selflessness; and then the superiority of the merit of selflessness is borrowed to conclude the earlier statement that a bodhisattva should thoroughly understand the dharma of selflessness. In the first half, though almsgiving of countless treasures, and even the giving of countless lives, are spoken of, none is called a bodhisattva; here alone a bodhisattva is named, from which one may know there must be a deep meaning. Read together with what follows and it becomes clear: this is a passage where each mirrors the other. For although this section speaks only of giving treasures, its meaning contains the fact that this person already knows all dharmas to be without self, and so is called a bodhisattva — but has not yet accomplished patience, and so does not equal the later bodhisattva. How is this known? Look at what follows: “this bodhisattva surpasses the merit attained by the former bodhisattva.”

In the first half, whether the giving of treasures or the giving of lives, the text speaks throughout of blessed merit, never of merit. Here, however, it says “the merit attained by the former bodhisattva.” That the former bodhisattva’s giving of the seven treasures is called merit means he must already know how to cultivate wisdom while apart from marks, and is not to be compared with one who only knows how to cultivate merit while clinging to marks. Because it says merit, it calls him a bodhisattva. Now one who has a self can never be apart from marks; so one knows the meaning contains the fact that this person already knows all dharmas to be without self. Moreover, it was said earlier: if a bodhisattva thoroughly understands the dharma of selflessness, the Tathāgata names him a true bodhisattva. Hence if one did not know dharmas to be without self, he would certainly not be called a bodhisattva. In sum, in this whole large section of the three on not receiving blessed merit, every word, every sentence, every name contains a most refined meaning and must not be slighted. “Worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges” means worlds equal in number to the river’s sands, that is, countless worlds. “With” means using; “filling” means completely filling — using the seven treasures that fill countless worlds to practice giving. This section merely cites one case of giving with abundant merit, to prepare the ground for the not receiving that follows.
(Chou) Second, comparing the superiority.
“And if again there is a person who understands that all dharmas are without self and attains accomplishment in patience, this bodhisattva surpasses the merit attained by the former bodhisattva.”

The bodhisattva who gives treasures in the text above already shadows forth the understanding that dharmas are without self. Here the bodhisattva who attains patience likewise shadows forth the giving of treasures. Look at the following phrases, “does not receive blessed merit,” “the blessed merit he creates,” and it becomes plainly evident that this bodhisattva greatly practices the blessed merit of giving. Because he greatly creates blessed merit yet does not receive it, he is said to attain accomplishment in patience. Otherwise, how could one know whether patience had been attained or not? Hence this section and the preceding one are beyond doubt passages where each mirrors the other. Once this meaning is clear, one knows that the sutra’s purport by no means makes light of blessed merit; one need only be unattached and not receive. Then the two phrases here, “understands that all dharmas are without self” and “attains accomplishment in patience,” are, in the sutra’s purport, really weighted toward the attaining of patience. I have seen several commentaries which, not understanding the meaning of each mirroring the other, took the phrase about accomplishing patience as an incidental remark, and so said that the former bodhisattva knew only how to cultivate merit while this bodhisattva knows dharmas to be without self, and therefore his merit surpasses the former’s — that cultivating merit is thus inferior to cultivating wisdom, and so on — greatly missing the sutra’s purport. Why? If that were the meaning, then what would become of the earlier earnest warning against the thought that one attains bodhi without cultivating blessed merit, as stated in the section “with respect to dharmas he does not speak of the mark of annihilation”? Most erroneous, most erroneous.

All dharmas are comprised in object, practice, and fruit. Object means the five aggregates, the six faculties, the six dusts, and so on; practice means the six pāramitās and all the ten thousand practices; fruit means the dwellings, practices, dedications, and grounds, up to supreme bodhi. “Without self” means that all dharmas, defiled and pure, are comprised in cause and effect. Cause and effect are precisely conditioned arising, and conditioned arising is empty in substance. Therefore within all dharmas there is originally no self. You should know that the so-called self is nothing else than the view of discrimination and clinging that living beings, in their ignorance and unenlightenment, falsely produce toward all dharmas. But the nature of all dharmas is originally empty and still — where could such a thing be? Because it is originally nonexistent, it should be removed. The knowing in “understands that all dharmas are without self” is understanding: it means grasping that the nature of all dharmas is originally empty and still. The five characters “all dharmas are without self” are the principle; the single character “knows” is the wisdom. “Attains accomplishment in patience” means that the principle that the nature of all dharmas is originally empty and still and without self, and the wisdom that knows it, can already be silently fused into one. Patience means acceptance, concord with no gap between — that is, being one. The union of principle and wisdom makes clear that self-clinging has been converted. When practice has reached this point, it is called accomplishment. How is it accomplished? Through permeating cultivation; hence “attains accomplishment.” To attain accomplishment is to say that permeating cultivation has issued in achievement. Without refinement of practice brought to the point, how could it be accomplished? So of these two phrases, the first is understanding and the second is practice; taken together, they make clear that this bodhisattva has accomplished both understanding and practice. Further, the first phrase, “knows,” is wisdom, and the second, “patience,” is concentration; joined, they are the equality of concentration and wisdom. Because his concentration and wisdom are equal, his understanding and practice are accomplished; and therefore the merit he attains surpasses that of the former bodhisattva. For the former bodhisattva’s understanding, practice, concentration, and wisdom had not yet reached the point of being silently fused into one; that is, the wisdom that knows had not yet reached the stage of resting settled and unmoved with respect to the principle that all dharmas are without self, and so he does not equal him. The meaning of the word patience in “understanding and practice” is likewise resting settled and unmoved.

From the earlier third large section, where it pointed out that if a bodhisattva thoroughly understands the dharma of selflessness the Tathāgata names him a true bodhisattva, the thread is only now concluded. From this one may know that everything said above is the dharma of selflessness, which bodhisattvas are made to understand thoroughly; but the work must be brought to the point of attaining accomplishment in patience before it is true thorough understanding and a true bodhisattva. Why? “Thorough” means clear penetration, which refers to understanding; “understanding” means arriving, which refers to practice. So to say “thoroughly understand” is to say that understanding and practice are complete. Because understanding and practice are complete, he is called a true bodhisattva. Hence the two characters “thoroughly understand” must not be taken as mere intellectual comprehension. You should know that understanding indeed comes before practice; yet without practicing according to the Dharma and truly experiencing it, how could one understand deeply? The earlier saying that practice comes forth from understanding and understanding is accomplished through practice — these two phrases are the true exposition of thorough understanding. Only by such thorough understanding does one attain accomplishment in patience.
(Zi) Second, making clear that it comes from his not receiving.
“Subhūti, because all bodhisattvas do not receive blessed merit.”

In the current circulating edition there is a “why” before Subhūti; Liu’s text and Hui’s edition lack it. Here there is already a word “because,” which sufficiently explains the meaning of the preceding text. What need is there to add “why”? I have seen several commentaries that say this section explains why the merit surpasses the former; a great error. The preceding text has already explained it: the merit surpasses the former because he has accomplished patience. What need of further explanation? You should know that this section uses the meaning of not receiving to explain the reason for accomplishing patience. For accomplishing patience is what is called realization. This section explains it, saying: what is meant by realization? Not receiving is.
