For the words “accomplishes patience” precisely teach students that the work must be brought to this point before one can be without self; hence the reason for accomplishing patience must be explained. As for the merit surpassing the former, that was originally an incidental remark — why specially explain it, especially when the preceding text has already explained it?

How is it that he does not receive? The meaning becomes clear in the next section. Meanwhile there is no harm in stating its essential purport. What is called not receiving is nothing else: it means that in widely practicing the six pāramitās of giving, one is as though nothing had happened. This none but one who can truly forget the self can manage. It means his practice has reached the point of pure, white-hot refinement, and so it is said he attains accomplishment. “All bodhisattvas” does not point to anyone in particular; it is like saying, every bodhisattva. “Because” means on account of. The sense is: every bodhisattva, because he cultivates merit without receiving it, accomplishes patience regarding selflessness. This bodhisattva likewise does not receive, and so is said to accomplish patience. The text above speaks of the merit he attains, and here speaks of not receiving blessed merit; this precisely makes clear that because he does not receive, the blessed merit he creates all becomes undefiled merit.

In the passage cited above, it does not say “giving the seven treasures filling countless worlds” but insists on “equal to the sands of the Ganges,” which also lodges a refined meaning. It makes clear that in the eyes of one who does not receive, such countless treasure-givings are equal to mud and sand — exceedingly slight, hardly worth mentioning. This is why he can not receive. If one regarded them as very many and very grand, one’s mind would already be turned by the object. When the mind has such an object, it is called receiving. To say here “does not receive” precisely makes clear that his mind is empty and has no object. Think it over, think it over — this too is a wondrous contemplation for one who would not receive and not cling.
(Gui) Second, making clear non-attachment. This has two parts: (Zi) first, requesting an explanation of the meaning; next, explaining non-attachment.
(Zi) First, requesting an explanation of the meaning.
Subhūti said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, how is it that a bodhisattva does not receive blessed merit?”

The Elder’s question has three senses. First, if one has already cultivated it and yet does not receive it, why cultivate it at all? He feared that those who did not grasp the meaning would fall into misunderstanding — this is the first sense of the question. Second, does “not receive” mean refusing and not accepting? When blessed merit comes, it is a settled principle of cause and effect; how could one refuse and not accept it? What then is meant by not receiving? This is the second sense. Third, it was said above that one attains patience through not receiving; but how can one not receive? The Elder asks in order that the great assembly may understand thoroughly and all reach the ground of not receiving — this is the third sense. Hence the words “Subhūti said to the Buddha” are especially set down, so that one may know the importance of this question; and one should attend with special care to the teaching of the next section.
(Zi) Second, explaining non-attachment.
“Subhūti, the blessed merit created by a bodhisattva should not be coveted or clung to; therefore it is said that he does not receive blessed merit.”

The first clause says “creates blessed merit,” so that one may know that although he does not receive it, he should create it. One must not, because of the word “not receive,” mistakenly think that cultivating merit may be slackened. You should know that creating blessed merit is precisely cultivating the six pāramitās, and comes forth from the mind of great compassion. All Buddhas and Tathāgatas take the mind of great compassion as their substance: because of living beings they bring forth great compassion; because of great compassion they give rise to the bodhi mind. How could it be slackened? The first sense of the question is thus resolved. Next, the three clauses say that because it should not be coveted and clung to, therefore it is said he does not receive — so that one may know that what is called not receiving is not refusing and not accepting, but simply not coveting and clinging. Not coveting and clinging means that whether blessed merit exists or not is never in one’s thoughts at all. For it makes clear that if one cultivates the six pāramitās in order to seek blessed merit, that is called coveting and clinging: it is benefiting oneself, not benefiting living beings; it is not the mind of great compassion and not supreme bodhi. Hence it should not be. Knowing this, the second sense of the question is resolved. To create blessed merit is not to cling to emptiness — it is great compassion. Not to covet and cling is not to cling to existence — it is great wisdom. With compassion and wisdom complete and clinging to neither emptiness nor existence, it is named the Middle Way. Moreover, to cling is to dwell; “should not covet and cling” is precisely “should dwell on nothing.” Joined with the preceding clause, it is precisely “should dwell on nothing and practice giving,” which exactly echoes what was said at the beginning of the sutra. And cultivating merit without clinging is also the meaning of the earliest saying: save all living beings to the end while there are none saved. All of this is for subduing self-clinging. The purport of this sutra lies in non-abiding and subduing the self; hence as it speaks down to the time of accomplishment and realization, it gathers back into non-abiding and subduing the self. Its spirit and purport run in one thread to the very bottom, without a single thread tangled.

Why then did the text above not simply say, “because all bodhisattvas do not covet and cling to blessed merit”? Would that not be direct and to the point? Why first say “does not receive” and then explain it by “not clinging”? You should know that the preceding section’s saying “does not receive” teaches how it is that one accomplishes patience; for accomplishing patience is what is meant by not receiving. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: ‘All non-receiving is named right receiving.’ Right receiving is samādhi; it is also called concentration, and also called patience. So the words “does not receive” are an essential gloss on the accomplishing of patience — how could they not be specially set out? As for the “not clinging” said here, it teaches how it is that one can not receive. In other words, the preceding section first tells us that the state of accomplishment and realization is total non-receiving; this section further tells us that the method of accomplishment and realization is nothing other than what was said at the sutra’s beginning: one should dwell on nothing and practice giving. How to realize and how to cultivate are pointed out most intimately and most essentially. Hence both statements, not receiving and not clinging, are indispensable.

Moreover, you should know that a practitioner should be unattached to everything. When the work of non-attachment is refined to fullness, it becomes non-receiving; so non-receiving too is total non-receiving. Here blessed merit is merely used to make the meaning clear. For the reason one receives is that one clings; the reason one clings is that one covets; the reason one covets is that there is a self. And what the self covets most is blessing. Hence the meaning is spoken with respect to blessed merit. Knowing this, the third sense of the question is resolved.

In sum, in the equal dharma-realm all dharmas are originally without self. The student should first open this right knowledge. Having known thus, he should practice thus. How should he practice? By what was said at the very first — one should dwell on nothing and practice giving — and by what is said here — the blessed merit one creates should not be coveted or clung to. In other words, it is to cultivate all dharmas widely while acting as though nothing were done. When after long time the work is refined to fullness, the mind is like empty space. Though one blazes forth in the practice of all dharmas, one is neither wearied nor tired of them, and one forgets them all in a vast nothingness — this is what is called not receiving. Not receiving describes a mind single and pure, unstained by the least mote of dust — and naturally so, not by force; constantly so, not by chance. Then compassion and wisdom are complete, concentration and wisdom equal, and the marks of self and the views of self born of discrimination and clinging are melted away to nothing. At this stage there is no name for it but to call it attaining accomplishment in patience. Yet this is still the bodhisattva’s state, not the Buddha’s. Hence what follows makes clear the empty marks of all dharmas, which are originally unborn. If one reaches the point of not a single thought arising, and even non-arising is absent, then one accords with and enters the Tathāgata’s equal dharma-realm. Hearing this essential purport, one should contemplate it in quiet.
(Xin) Second, making clear the empty marks of all dharmas and concluding that dharmas are unborn.

The text that follows is precisely where every drop returns to the source. Hence its meaning is very broad, very deep, and very fine. If one merely explained the text itself, bound by the words, one could not speak it through; and how then could the hearer hear it through? The only way is first to unfold the essential purport it contains to the fullest. Then when one comes to the text itself, a few words suffice. This too is one method of expounding profound principles.

All that has been said above, a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, is covered by one word: non-abiding. What is non-abiding? It is what is called not dwelling in marks. Why not dwell in marks? Because, as is said, if the mind grasps marks, then it clings to self, person, being, and life. You should know that to be free of dwelling in marks, the mind must not grasp. Not grasping is precisely for breaking the self; and breaking the self is precisely for realizing the one true dharma-realm of one suchness and equality. This one dharma-realm is the permanently abiding, unmoving Dharmakāya, which is called the Tathāgata.

In sum, the meaning spoken throughout the sutra is contained in the eight characters: not grasping at marks, such and unmoved. It is only at the very end that these eight characters are pointed out plainly. For this reason, the sutra meaning of this large section on the empty marks of all dharmas is spoken by fusing the whole sutra’s purport and carrying it to the ultimate and thorough. This is what is called every drop returning to the source. Hence what it says is the more perfect and the more wondrous.

Thus the whole sutra speaks of selflessness, and here it says that selflessness is originally nonexistent. If even selflessness is absent, then non-abiding too is non-abiding, and not grasping too is not grasping. Why? Because all dharmas are originally unborn. And there is no such thing as unborn either. Why? Because dharmas are precisely non-dharmas, and marks are precisely non-marks. Only then is there ultimate selflessness — and selflessness too is absent.

From this one may know that the meanings spoken above — no holy and no ordinary, neither one nor different — are precisely: in the very midst of holy and ordinary, no holy and no ordinary; just as one and different, yet not one and different; forgetting that it is non-receiving, and so naming it non-receiving. Hence although there is no holy and no ordinary, it does not hinder becoming holy or ordinary; and although one becomes holy or ordinary, it is still no holy and no ordinary. One and different, and all the rest, are each like this.

Then there is no such thing as two extremes, no such thing as clinging, no such thing as a middle. Why? If even the one does not stand, how could there be two, much less extremes or a middle? Yet it is not that they are utterly nonexistent: though the ten thousand existents are manifold, existence is precisely nonexistence. Why? Because they are originally unborn — this is what is called suchness, what is called unmoved, what is called not grasping.

For to give rise to a mind that does not grasp is already grasping! To give rise to a mind that is unmoved — that mind has long since moved! To give rise to a mind that is such — what suchness could remain? To give rise to a mind that removes the self — then the view of self and the mark of self stand stark before one. If one does not know how to take the point here, then however bitterly and diligently one cultivates, in the end one is only going round and round and adding vines and brambles.

In sum, what this large section says is precisely the utmost unfolding of “not grasping at marks, such and unmoved,” carried to the ultimate. It is where students are led to contemplate deep prajñā; it is where all living beings are made to attain great freedom. Since the sutra text darts its gaze in all directions and is lucid on every face, the hearer too should dart his gaze in all directions and be lucid on every face. One must not die beneath the words and be turned about by the text. One should gather one’s spirit and empty one’s mind, and receive every word and every sentence at the place where no thought has yet stirred. If one sticks fast to the least mark of discursive seeking or of names, there is no way in.

What I said a moment ago, that one should take the point here — not shrinking from vines and brambles, let me repeat it to make it plain. The heading “empty marks” contains two meanings: originally without marks, and not grasping marks. For this large section speaks precisely of the principle-substance, and precisely of the work of cultivation. The practitioner should first understand that the principle-substance is originally without marks, and therefore one should not grasp marks. And since the substance is without marks, one who cultivates non-grasping should at every time and in every place contemplate the principle-substance of all dharmas, which is originally without marks. This is what is called raising the whole of cultivation from the whole of the nature, and the whole of cultivation resting in the nature.

Since that is so, one who would learn the prajñā practice of non-abiding need not be confined to beginning the cultivation from the start; one may begin directly from the empty marks of all dharmas. Hence it is said that one should take the point here.

You should know that the perfect teaching of the Great Vehicle has gradations and also has no gradations. Hence the Chan school says: “point directly upward.” “Upward” means tending toward the source. “Point directly” means cutting away branches and leaves, fixing the eye on the source at a single glance, and going straight in with a single blade. If one takes this saying woodenly and thinks that only the Dharma-door of investigating the meditative topic can contemplate thus and enter directly, while those who recite the Buddha’s name or practice other Dharma-doors cannot do this work of contemplating the source, then one loses the good benefit oneself — what loss could be greater?

In a sutra of definitive meaning, not one sentence is less than thorough, not one dharma is other than from head to tail complete. Where it speaks of principle is where it speaks of cultivation, and it runs straight through to the realization of the fruit. Teaching, principle, practice, and fruit, though divided into four, if one insisted that they are four separate matters, would that not mean that apart from practice and fruit there is a separate teaching and principle — and what teaching and principle would be worth speaking of then? For this reason, in a sutra of definitive meaning, every phrase can realize the Way and every sentence can be a gate of entry.

Take the Amitābha Sutra. The two phrases “holding fast to the name” and “single-mindedness undisturbed” are indeed said to have a before and after: the phrase “holding fast” is where one sets to work, and the phrase “single-minded” is the effect of holding fast. Yet if one cannot comprehend the single mind in order to begin the cultivation, one will in the end fail to accomplish the holding fast. How then can single-mindedness undisturbed be regarded merely as an effect?

As for this sutra: every sentence speaks principle and speaks cultivation, and there is no sentence that cannot run through the entire sutra. How could this one section alone be so? Hence, take up any sentence at random, and one may awaken to the Way through it. Once the Sixth Patriarch of the Chan school heard the line “he should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing” and thereby awakened completely. Later people insisted that of the whole sutra this one line alone is the most wondrous — this is precisely what is called turning about at another’s heels.

If one is truly a clever fellow and knows that the Great Vehicle Buddha’s teaching is a Dharma-seal, then one may take up any sentence at random and seal every matter and every dharma with it. In other words, one brings every matter and every dharma to be understood in the light of this Dharma-seal — only thus is one a person who knows how to apply the work. Then walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are never apart from this, and one easily gains true benefit. How much more so with this large section, where every sentence speaks of the source of the mind. What the Buddha realized, He realized this. If one thought this to be the Tathāgata’s state, beyond the reach of beginners — should a student then not turn the light back upon the source of his own mind? That such a view is a great error needs no saying.

To turn the light back upon the source of the mind is indeed no easy matter. Yet if one does not contemplate at the source but goes seeking among branches and leaves, how can one cultivate well? If one can contemplate and enter the source even a little, all the work of cultivation can be split apart like a bamboo meeting the blade. This is like one who studies letters: if he gains a little of the style of the classics, the philosophers, and the men of Qin and Han, he stands out above others from the first stroke. Cultivation is likewise; one should know it thus. The ancient worthies said: one must not exalt the sage’s realm too high and so give rise to self-abasement — a truly pressing saying.

blocks.text: Section Twenty-Nine: The Stillness of Majestic Deportment

inline.s: (Xin) This section has two parts: (Ren) first, dissolving marks and entering the substance; next, concluding that there is no arising. (Ren) first has three parts: (Gui) first, making clear, with respect to the sage’s title, being apart from coming and going; next, making clear, with respect to the dust-realms, being apart from one and many; third, making clear, with respect to the view of self, being apart even from being apart. (Gui) first has two parts: (Zi) first, rebuking ordinary feeling; next, explaining the right meaning.
(Zi) First, rebuking ordinary feeling.
“Subhūti, if anyone says that the Tathāgata comes, goes, sits, or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.”

The phrase “the empty marks of all dharmas” is the Great Vehicle’s Dharma-seal. The phrases “neither coming nor going” and the rest are all Dharma-seals. A Dharma-seal means that every dharma can be sealed and settled by this meaning. Here it is merely made clear with respect to the Tathāgata’s title, by way of example. You should know that coming and going and the rest are all confronting marks of things. One who would realize the absolute substance must dissolve all opposites and empty out their illusory marks. Why? Because the nature of all dharmas is originally without marks. This makes clear, with respect to the nature-substance, that all dharmas are originally of empty marks. If one speaks of the empty marks of all dharmas with respect to the work of cultivation, it means emptying out the marks of all dharmas — which is the meaning of dissolving marks and entering the substance.

The Tathāgata is a name for the virtue of the intrinsic nature. But this person clings to the word “comes,” and if there is coming there must be going; and having coming and going, he further associates sitting and lying down. This makes clear that if one clings to a single mark, it will inevitably draw on more and more, until the ten thousand marks are in confusion and one can never attain purity. It shows that in reading the sutras and hearing the Dharma one must not cling to the marks of words. This person is wholly outside the gate: hearing the name Tathāgata, his mind at once seems to have a coming and going, and walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, each mark different from the next.

The four occurrences of “or” depict a mind turning after marks, arising and ceasing without pause, as though something were seen, its expression painted. One who speaks thus measures the sage’s realm by ordinary feeling and has not understood the meaning of Tathāgata at all. Hence: “that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.” The word “I” refers to the Tathāgata, meaning that he does not understand the meaning made clear by the two characters Tathāgata; it may also refer to the Buddha. Wherever the Buddha teaches Dharma, it is always to make people leave marks and realize the nature; even words and language must not be clung to. This person knows nothing of the nature and clings to names and phrases; he has not the least grasp of the Buddha’s meaning. Hence: “he does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.” The rebuke of this person’s failure to understand is precisely meant to make everyone understand deeply the purport of empty marks.
(Zi) Second, explaining the right meaning.
“Why? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore he is called the Tathāgata.”

The Tathāgata is the Dharmakāya. The Dharmakāya permanently abides and does not move; there is no such thing as coming and going. The Dharmakāya pervades every place, and has no need of coming and going. What is seen as coming and going is only the response-transformation body. This body is a dharma of conditioned arising: it is said to arise following the conditions of living beings’ faculties and responses. In other words, this manifested body is so only as seen through the eyes of living beings; the Tathāgata has never moved at all. This is what is called conditioned arising. How is this made clear? Consider: the Buddha has manifested — why is it that some living beings see him and some do not? Why is it that sometimes they see him and sometimes they do not? Whether he is seen or not depends entirely on how the minds of living beings are. When the mind is pure, the Buddha appears, and it is named coming; when the mind is turbid, the Buddha hides, and it is named going. Purity and turbidity of mind rest wholly with living beings; hence the hiding and appearing of the response-transformation body likewise rests wholly with living beings. So it is said to arise following conditions. Yet where there is a condition there must also be a cause. What is the cause? It is what was earlier called the power of the root of kindness and the accomplishment of the two kinds of wisdom. Therefore it appears the moment there is a response, without giving rise to a thought or a notion; therefore although it manifests in every direction, it is as though nothing had happened, and the Dharmakāya’s unmoving remains as it was, never dwelling in the marks of coming and going. Yet although the Dharmakāya does not move, it constantly manifests the response-transformation body without ever ceasing, and likewise does not dwell in the unmoving substance. This is what is called such and unmoved.

It makes clear that although it is such, it is unmoved; and although it is unmoved, it is such. Hence although coming and going are seen, in truth there is no coming and going; and although there is no coming and going, it does not hinder the seeing of coming and going. Here it says: comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. It does not mean that there is ultimately no coming and going; it means that coming has no place and going has no place. The two words “nowhere” are the most important. “Nowhere” means no place: it describes the Dharmakāya as originally pervading every place — how could it have a place of coming or a place of going? Since there is coming and going yet no place of coming and going, one may see that although there is coming and going, there has in fact never been coming and going; rather, without ever coming or going, it appears as coming and going. This meaning is precisely dwelling while not dwelling, and not dwelling while dwelling. It is the utmost of being apart from marks. Why? Because the marks both of coming and going and of not coming and going are alike left behind; hence it is called the utmost.

In sum, coming and going are seen from the standpoint of neither coming nor going, and neither coming nor going is seen from the standpoint of coming and going. Not only are all marks that have marks left behind; all marks that are without marks are left behind too. For true suchness and true marks are originally thus. As for true suchness: there is nothing to dismiss, and so it is called true; and there is nothing to establish, and so it is called such. As for true marks: though without marks, it is also not without marks. Hence the conclusion: therefore he is called the Tathāgata. “Called” means provisionally named. Not only is “coming” a provisional name; “such” is a provisional name too. Why? To say that true suchness “comes” is to say that it does not dwell in nirvāṇa. For the substance of true suchness is originally unmoved, and yet it is now said to come; so what is called “such” is a name and nothing more — it in truth does not dwell in the unmoved true suchness. And since it comes, it is said to be “such,” which is to say that it does not dwell in birth and death. For the marks of coming and going are birth and death, and yet it is now said to be such; so what is called “coming” is likewise a name and nothing more — it in truth does not dwell in the coming and going of birth and death. All this is simply to make clear that its selflessness is utter: it responds as soon as there is a sense of it, appears when conditions meet, with no room in it for anything at all. To have no room for anything is to say that not a single thought arises. If thought has not even arisen, how could the mind ever have moved?

Although this section makes the meaning clear with respect to the Dharmakāya, in fact the meaning of the two bodies is made clear as well. One who understands thoroughly should turn and contemplate his own five-aggregate body of form: though it has coming and going, the Buddha-nature intrinsically possessed in truth neither comes nor goes. Then one may enter by way of neither coming nor going.

Those marks of coming and going — how are they worth entertaining in thought? Once one has entered and merged with the nature-substance, one may simply let them come and go and manifest marks; why entertain them in thought at all? Then one neither grasps nor annihilates, and negation and illumination are simultaneous.
